subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker -and I apologize for not having given you an opportunity to put the motion-I think it is desirable, as the Prime Minister has already indicated, that the views of the house on this matter might be made known to him and the government before he departs for the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London.
Before dealing with this matter in the context of the commonwealth, perhaps I may be permitted on behalf of the official opposition -as this will be the last opportunity before he leaves-to convey to the Prime Minister our good wishes for his mission and our best hopes for a happy and successful sojourn in London.
Along with that wish we express our hopes that this conference, to which I know the Prime Minister will make an important contribution for Canada, will result especially at this time, as other commonwealth conferences in the past have resulted, in strengthening good and constructive relationships within the commonwealth so that the members of the commonwealth may continue to play an even stronger and more constructive part for peace in the world.
I understand, though I have no official confirmation of the fact, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) will be leaving with the Prime Minister to attend a meeting of the NATO council in Turkey, I believe. If that is the case I should like to include him in our good wishes for a successful and profitable journey. I am sure the deliberations of the NATO council at this particular time will be as significant as on any occasion in the past. It is of great importance to all of us that these deliberations should result in strengthening NATO and trying to work out a common NATO policy on the eve of the summit conference. I hope-


indeed, I know-that the minister will do his part at this NATO council meeting to bring about that result.
I am sure the commonwealth meeting in London will not only be an important one, but in the circumstances of today perhaps in some ways it will be an uneasy and even difficult one. The commonwealth has, of course, faced its difficulties before now and surmounted them. I believe this will be the first meeting of commonwealth prime ministers since July, 1957, and in view of the complexity and difficulty of the subjects which will face the prime ministers perhaps our own Prime Minister may conceivably have changed his mind, as expressed on one occasion, that there should be a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers every year if practicable, I think he added, which is an important addition.
The value of the informal character of these commonwealth prime ministers' conferences-and I stress the word "informal"- is admitted, especially by anyone who has had the privilege and responsibility of taking part in them. Very often they have no specific agenda at all or in the sense at least that controversial subjects are rarely put on any agenda unless they are agreed to in advance. But whatever may be the nature of the formal agenda or lack of it, informal discussions customarily do take place at meetings of this kind on the most controversial and difficult subjects; and they can be, of course, and in the past have been on more than one occasion, the most important discussions that take place.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that recent developments in South Africa make it desirable and, indeed, I should think make it inevitable that, whatever may be the nature of the formal agenda, at least informally and perhaps in a very important way these developments should be considered. I agree, Mr. Speaker, that based on the experience of the past, it would be a mistake to formalize agendas at meetings of this kind; but I think it would even be a greater mistake at this time not to take advantage of the opportunity of exchanging views informally on this and every other matter of interest, however controversial, to the member governments and member peoples of the commonwealth.
The effort to formalize and organize the commonwealth itself through centralized institutions would have prevented its development at all and, if it had been persisted in, I think might well have resulted in its disappearance in its present form. There were those in this country and in other countries who, with the very best of intentions and desires, sought that kind of commonwealth growth. However, I think it is

fortunate for the commonwealth that any effort in that direction was not successful. If such an effort in the twenties and early thirties-and I am talking now about centralizing and institutionalizing the commonwealth-was not successful, it would be, of course, quite impossible now because of the very nature of the membership, with governments having different foreign policies and indeed very different international commitments. So the commonwealth today is a close and family association without the binding commitments which it sometimes undertakes through formal treaty obligations.
There have been great changes, of course, in this association. There have been changes from the old British empire to the first British commonwealth brought about in the twenties and sealed by the Statute of Westminster in 1932, I think it was. There were changes from the first British commonwealth of nations in the thirties to the second commonwealth of nations which developed after world war II. Indeed, the shrinking of the old British empire into the present commonwealth in a sense represents its greatest achievement; for out of this empire, have peacefully emerged by evolution those free nations which make up our new and enlarged commonwealth today. That emergence has taken more than one form and has expressed itself in more than one way. It is well that we should be clear about this matter as the commonwealth faces perhaps some difficult problems in the days ahead.
Some of the members-Canada, Australia and New Zealand-have grown from colonies to independent states, with strong ties of race, sentiment, history and heritage still linking them to the mother country long after they have achieved full self-government. But other nations of the commonwealth have an entirely different historical basis for membership in this association. South Africa, which is very much in our minds today, became a member out of its defeat in war and out of British magnanimity and statesmanship in victory. India, Pakistan, Ceylon and Malaya were British colonies but with old cultures and civilizations of their own, anteceding those indeed of the mother country itself. These ancient nations and modern colonies and now independent states-and we sometimes forget this-learned a great deal from the British. They learned of the rule of law, even-handed justice, fair dealing, administrative and governmental order and methods. Indeed, it was the British, even though they may not have been very conscious of it at the time, who also gave them a sense of national
27, 1960	3321
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth consciousness which, in some cases, they had never possessed before. It was on this basis that their freedom developed.
There is also now a native African member of the commonwealth, and very soon there are likely to be others along with a West Indies federation and perhaps a Mediterranean island. Their peoples have never in the past had a cohesive national identity or a continuous national story as we understand it, but they have nevertheless now become independent, indigenous states with only in some cases a few white Britishers to recall the previous political connection with Whitehall.
All this means that there has been a fundamental change from empire to commonwealth, and there has been an equally important change from old commonwealth to new commonwealth. It is this new multiracial commonwealth which exists today, representing every clime, every religion and almost every culture. Four fifths of the people who make up this new commonwealth are Asian, a fact which has an important bearing on the troubles in South Africa. This new commonwealth includes the second most populous country in the world and the second most populous Moslem state. It represents three of the ancient civilizations of mankind, namely Judeo-Christian, Hindu and Islam. Inside it there are four monarchies by choice and conviction. There are three nations that have stated their intention of becoming republics. There are two that actually are republics and there is one, an elected monarchy, where the local monarch-and I am referring to Malaya -accepts another monarch in London as the head of the association. It must seem all very confusing to any logical student of political forms and organizations, but in its way it works. It has worked well in the past, and we hope it will work even better in its new sphere in the future.
The commonwealth has adjusted itself pragmatically and on the whole gracefully to a long series of changing circumstances. Yet it would be folly-and I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will not accuse me of being pessimistic when I say this-to become complacent about what has been done or to assume that this beneficent progress must inevitably and automatically continue. There is no certainty today that it will do so, although we hope it will. It would also be foolish to try to obscure the new problems facing us in a haze of patriotic oratory, As the United Kingdom prime minister himself said on his return from Africa, I think
3322	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth it was about the end of January-and I quote from the press report of a statement he made on his return:
We mustn't take the commonwealth for granted. We could easily break it up or throw it away.
There are undoubtedly difficulties ahead and Africa has shown that they can develop into dangers for the commonwealth association. But there are also opportunities for even greater service of this multiracial association; to its members and to the world-
I therefore think, and I am sure all members in the house will agree with me on this matter, that it remains an important objective of Canada's policy to help avoid the dangers ahead and to help realize the full opportunities of the commonwealth association. It should be a privilege for any Canadian to work for the maintenance and strengthening of this commonwealth of nations as a strong force for peace, security and progress in the world of 1960.
Mr. Speaker, there is one particular and special difficulty very much in our minds, which is referred to in this resolution, which confronts us and the commonwealth today. That is the policy of apartheid in the Union of South Africa. I am sure that difficulty will be very much in the minds of the commonwealth prime ministers when they are in London, as it is also in our minds in this parliament today as well as in the minds of the people of Canada.
Apartheid is a policy founded on racial segregation, on racial discrimination, on racial privilege on the one hand and racial inferiority on the other. Any person who has any affinity at all with liberal views-and I use the word "liberal" with the smallest of "l's"-must protest against that kind of policy wherever it might be found in the world, especially if it were found in any of its aspects in our own country. Because it is a policy of differentiation based on race and colour. It is a policy of separate development, and it has been applied in South Africa in a strict, determined, and I believe narrow way. It is a policy particularly offensive to the other members of the commonwealth, especially those in Africa and in Asia who make up four fifths of the people of this association.
This question of apartheid has over the years been before the United Nations for international consideration. So far as the period during which I, as a member of a government, had some responsibility is concerned, I recall that the Canadian delegation at the United Nations joined other delegations in condemnation of the policy of racial discrimination but were cautious about condemning South Africa itself. In those earlier


years we hoped that more liberal trends, more liberal policies and more liberal people, if you like, in South Africa would get stronger in their influence and that the South Africans themselves would remove any legitimate causes of international complaint.
We feared in those days that outright and formal condemnation of the South African government, quite apart from any special problem or difficulty arising out of the commonwealth association, would weaken rather than strengthen these liberal forces by rallying all white South Africans behind their government and its policy in the face of attack from outside, because that kind of attack by condemnation from outside very often has that effect inside. We hoped, then, that Canadian and other commonwealth influences could be used as opportunity offered to impress on South Africa that the policy of apartheid was wrong, that it could not succeed; that it was hurting South Africa itself and should be changed. Any such intervention or friendly pressure of that kind would of course have been made difficult then, if not impossible, by supporting outright strong and formal condemnation of South Africa itself at the United Nations.
Mr. Speaker, whatever may have been the situation earlier, whatever may have been the considerations which at that time seemed to prompt caution, whatever may have been our hopes in those days, in the light of later developments, recent developments especially, it is surely no longer possible to refrain from speaking out; because these recent developments have shown depressingly and conclusively that the hoped for evolution in the right direction has not been taking place. Indeed, these most recent developments, have confirmed among other things, what was becoming increasingly evident, that South African policy was moving, if it were moving at all, in the wrong direction.
So there was bound to be violence, and it culminated in the tragedy of Sharpeville, an event that shocked the conscience of the world; at least that part of the conscience of the world which has the right to express itself in freedom. That tragedy and subsequent events, as I have already stated outside this house, should cause dismay and distress to us all.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this matter has been referred to during this session. It was brought up on January 29 by my hon. friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who, dealing with apartheid, asked the Prime Minister, as reported on page 491 of Hansard, whether he did not think, in view of the character of these meetings-that is, the commonwealth meetings in London, with their

secrecy-that this was among the kind of questions that should be discussed, as they have been discussed, among the prime ministers of the commonwealth.
This question was referred to later, on February 11, by myself, when I had this to say as reported on page 983 of Hansard:
I do not think anybody in this house, certainly nobody in this party, would wish to take any course of action which would drive South Africa out of the commonwealth, but we surely do not wish to see a course followed by South Africa which will drive four fifths of the people in the commonwealth outside the commonwealth.
Then on March 23 I asked the Prime Minister whether, having had an opportunity to examine the reports from South Africa, he could express the distress and dismay of this parliament at the violence which was used in South Africa in measures taken in connection with a coloured demonstration against the racial policies of the South African government, which violence resulted in such tragic loss of life. The Prime Minister replied that he had not received the report he had requested through diplomatic channels, and that until he had done so he thought it would be inappropriate to make any statement except to reiterate the fact-and I here quote from Hansard, page 2349-
-that we deplore the development of a situation which has given rise to such tragic violence and loss of life.
Then on March 25 I asked the Prime Minister whether he had received the report in question and whether he had any statement to make. He replied, as reported on page 2448 of Hansard:
The conclusion of the government is that at this time no beneficial purpose would be served by diplomatic protests or by even more extreme measures to intervene in this tragic situation.
Then on March 31 I asked the Prime Minister whether he would instruct the Canadian representative in South Africa to inform the South African government of the alarm and distress of this parliament at political developments which had led to such violence and might lead to anarchy. The Prime Minister replied that the views that had been expressed in this chamber in recent days had been made known to the representative of South Africa in Ottawa.
Then on April 1 I asked the Prime Minister whether he would make provision to express the views of this parliament through a resolution on the policy of apartheid, and provision has now been made for a discussion of the matter.
Mr. Speaker, I think one of the first questions we should ask ourselves as we discuss this matter is this. Have we the right in the Canadian parliament to intervene and express
27. 1960	3323
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth our views and have those views made known to the government of South Africa? I think we have not only that right, but now we have that duty.
It has been suggested in some quarters that if the governments of the commonwealth took irresponsible or drastic or strong action it might drive South Africa out of the commonwealth. Certainly that is not the purpose of anything I am saying today, and I hope it is not the purpose of any hon. member of this house. But we cannot refuse to face the situation-it is one which, I hope, will not materialize-that South Africa may drive herself out of the commonwealth by forcing a choice between her policies and the views of other members. I read only this morning a report from Kuala Lumpur in Malaya which underlines this danger. Perhaps this is the kind of danger which the prime ministers' conference to be held in London may be able to avoid. Before he left for London the Prime Minister of Malaya, with the unanimous support of his parliament, said he was going to raise this question in London, and he added these words which I quote from a Reuters dispatch:
If South Africa chooses to get out of the commonwealth as a result of my actions, then I say "good riddance".
That, surely, is the sort of thing which the right kind of intervention by the parliaments of the commonwealth could perhaps prevent rather than bring about. Therefore the purpose of this intervention on my part is to express my own views and the views of my party on this matter in the hope that this kind of expression and intervention may help to correct the situation in South Africa which, if it is not corrected, may have the worst kind of result for the commonwealth association.
Our Prime Minister is reported as having said toward the end of January of this year to a delegation of the Canadian Labour Congress-and I quote from the press report-
The essence of the commonwealth is the independence of its members. I ask you what would be our reaction in Canada if some other part of the commonwealth were to criticize us.
Up to a point I agree entirely with that. We have to be careful and responsible before we indulge in idle criticism of not only other members of the commonwealth but other friendly states. But surely this situation in South Africa now has gone beyond the point of no criticism.

speechtext:
I remember that. It came up in the house, and the Prime Minister made it clear he would not subscribe to any purpose or action of that kind. I think I have already indicated my agreement on that point. Now the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, who is as responsible and careful in these matters as, I think, any leader of a government could be, speaking in Capetown to the South African parliament itself in January of this year had this to say-perhaps I may quote from what he is reported to have said-
In this shrinking world in which we live today, the internal policies of one nation may have effects outside it. We may sometimes be tempted to say to each other, "Mind your own business". But, in these days, I would myself expand the old saying so that it runs "Mind your own business, but mind how it affects my business, too."
Let me be very frank with you, my friends-
Remember, he is talking to the South African parliament.
As a fellow member of the commonwealth, it is our earnest desire to give South Africa our support and encouragement, but I hope you won't mind my saying frankly that there are some aspects of your policies which make it impossible for us to do this without being false to our own deep convictions about the political destinies of free men-
That was a courageous statement, particularly in view of the fact that it was made in South Africa. Thus, I say, we have not only the right but the duty to criticize, publicly dissociate ourselves from and, indeed, protest against the apartheid policies of the government of South Africa.
The correspondent of the London Observer in Johannesburg had this to say on April 23- last Saturday-and I quote from his report:
The recent crisis has heen settled in a way that takes South Africa closer to revolution; it has now entered a shadowy period of complete uncertainty. This is the moment for constructive international influence to make itself felt-
It is no longer possible to argue that what happens in South Africa is not a threat to world peace. It is most decidedly so, and the west should act accordingly.
Certainly domestic violence in that part of the world can become a threat to international order and international peace; and any policy of white supremacy, colour discrimination and race segregation based on the doctrine of apartheid is bound to result in violence. Perhaps I might be permitted to quote what I said on this point outside the house. I said:
Such a policy can only lead to tragedy which will engulf the white minority as well as the coloured majority. It may lead even to anarchy. The South African government should know how Canadians feel about this.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

In taking our stand against these policies and the principles on which they are based, we in Canada have no reason to be smug or superior. It would be hypocritical on our part to praise ourselves that we are not as other men: if we had faced conditions that other people have had to face, who have racial problems that we know nothing of, our record might not be as good as it is.
Our country is not twisted by discords of the past or torn by racial enmities handed down as part of history. We have few of the national prejudices and ancient grudges that, in other and older countries, maintain and foster enmities and suspicions. But who can say that we are free from intolerance and discrimination and bigotry?
So let us avoid any trace of smug holier than thou superiority-nevertheless, it is true-and we have the right to say it-that any governmental policy in any country which is based on racial superiority or discrimination will not succeed but in time will lead only to disaster.
No government, no nation, can have security, peace and progress in the future which bases its policy of the present on these false, wrong and evil assumptions.
We Canadians have the right, and indeed the duty, to condemn strongly and clearly what we cannot approve, remembering that condemnation of these things in other countries will have a hollow ring if we permit them in any shape or form at home.
So our condemnation, our protest, must be constructive and even understanding, and not merely captious and emotional. I do not pretend to know very much about South Africa. Indeed, I know very little except from what I have been able to read and study; but surely any student of history, ancient or contemporary, is bound to come to the conclusion that there must be a change in South African policy before it is too late or the events of recent weeks will be nothing to what will happen in the months ahead. The winds of change are blowing in that part of the world and those who do not recognize this will be blown away. Time surely is not on the side of the white South Africans in this matter any more than the facts and the tides of contemporary history are on their side. What may have been possible, even if it were not right, 50 years ago is now neither right nor possible.
There are deep, dark forces at work which may soon sweep away the chances of any settlement based on reason and justice. This becomes more likely as the moderate, reasonable and more experienced non-white leaders in South Africa-along with white leaders of the opposition to apartheid-are now being jailed. All history shows that in these circumstances there is only one result; the forces and the leaders of extremism and of violence take over even though they may temporarily be driven underground. There are also, no doubt, externally controlled subversive elements present in South Africa who are happy to exploit the situation and happy to see the South African government make easier their task.

Back in 1909 when the British House of Commons was considering the bill to give South Africa self-government as a union- that bill and that action was a great tribute to the magnanimity and farsighted wisdom of Great Britain-a Liberal member of that day-I think his name was Mr. Byles-had this to say, and I quote from the Hansard of that time:
A gulf, a widening and dangerous gulf is being fixed between black and white. Some day they will hear the call of their blood.
That call is becoming a cry as blood is being shed. In that poignant, moving story of South Africa by Alan Paton, "Cry, the Beloved Country", which no doubt many hon. members have read, the author has one of his characters say:
I fear that when we whites learn to love you Africans, you will have learned to hate us.
How can there be any other result if a government in 1960 insists with obstinate determination, yes, with a fierce sincerity, and even in some cases with religious conviction, on applying the policies of apartheid to three quarters of its people, at a time when the universal declaration of human rights has been accepted by all governments as a solemn commitment and by all peoples as their due. In these unhappy circumstances this house has a right and, I repeat, a duty to make its views known clearly and strongly, but with responsibility. I give these views as I see them in the hope that they may commend themselves to the house, and I summarize them as follows. We deplore and protest against the policy of apartheid of the government of South Africa under which persons because of race and colour are denied by law human rights and fundamental freedoms. We have watched with anxiety and dismay this policy lead to arbitrary arrests and detentions without trial, to unrest and violence. We believe that its continuance seriously threatens those relations of confidence and friendship which are necessary for any continued and constructive association between members of the commonwealth.
We are convinced that peace and order in any country can in the long run be secured and maintained only on the basis of freedom and non-discrimination and on full respect for the dignity and worth of all men, whatever their race, colour or creed.
I venture to express the hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he goes to London may see fit to make known views of this kind or views which may be more appropriately expressed than the way in which I have tried to express them, not only to the delegate of South Africa but to all the members of that conference as representing the views of this parliament of Canada
27. 1960	3325
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth and that he also may see fit to send views of this kind directly to the South African government through the diplomatic channels.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding to deal with the motion which is before the house may I take the liberty of thanking the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for the good wishes he extended to me in respect of my trip to the NATO foreign ministers' meeting in Istanbul, Turkey at the commencement of next week. It always helps a great deal, as I am sure that hon. gentleman found by experience, to be able to go to these meetings feeling that one has behind him the encouraging thoughts of his fellow members of parliament. I am very hopeful that some worth-while progress will be made during the course of these meetings.
In addition to the ordinary NATO meetings there is to be a meeting of the five foreign ministers of the western countries which are members of the ten-member disarmament committee, for the purpose of preparing the case on disarmament for the chiefs of state and heads of government who will represent the west at the summit meeting on May 16. This particular work, too, is of great importance and I am hopeful that one result will be that more progress will be made in the field of disarmament during the weeks that lie ahead.
The subject under discussion today is one which has touched the emotions and the consciences of all Canadians very deeply. In the heat of political statements there have been some suggestions made that the members of the government are not as much concerned and upset about this problem as they might be. In this connection I should like to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), house leader of the C.C.F., when speaking in this house on March 25, 1960 as reported at page 2453 of Hansard. The hon. member said:
From my associations with hon. members opposite and from the public statements of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs I can say that I know of no one in this chamber who condones what is being done in South Africa.
The Leader of the Opposition has taken that same position in his remarks this afternoon and that is an accurate statement of the feelings of every member of parliament sitting here today.
Unfortunately there have been quite violent criticisms of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on this point and I have found them very difficult to understand because throughout his whole career in public life he has been against discrimination of any kind.
3326	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth
May I say on this point, too, that I do not think there is a member in the house who believes down in his heart that the Prime Minister of Canada is not frightfully disturbed about this South African question and just as strongly opposed to discrimination of any kind as he has been throughout his career. This had been shown during the course of the last three weeks right here in the house. I would refer, for example, to the first occasion when the question was raised, which was on March 22. I am reading from page 2299 of Hansard. The Prime Minister had this to say:
The attitude of the Canadian government has been made clear on more than one occasion, that anything in the nature of racial discrimination is not regarded favourably and is indeed condemned.
On March 23, in answer to a further question, he said this, and this particular extract was read by the Leader of the Opposition in the course of his speech a few moments ago. I am reading from page 2341 of Hansard:
It would be inappropriate to make any statement, except to reiterate the fact that we deplore the development of a situation which has given rise to such tragic violence and loss of life.
Two days later, on March 25, the Prime Minister said, and I am quoting from page 2448 of Hansard:
I have already made it clear on numerous occasions that the government has no sympathy for policies of racial discrimination and that we deplore the development of a situation which has given rise to such tragic violence and loss of life.
There were further similar statements, one in particular on March 31, when the Prime Minister was being questioned by the Leader of the Opposition, and I am quoting from page 2641 of Hansard:
The house will be aware, from the statements I have made in this house since the recent disturbances began, of how profoundly the government regrets and deplores the tragic situation which prevails in that country.
The Prime Minister was referring to South Africa. I continue:
I should add, too, that the views that have been expressed in this chamber in recent days have been made known to the representative of South Africa in Ottawa.
I can vouch for that latter statement, as I had made those views known myself to the acting high commissioner for South Africa. Then, on April 11, after Mr. Norman Phillips, Canadian newsman, had been arrested in South Africa, the Prime Minister had this to say, as found at page 3087 of Hansard:
The matter was taken up with me, acting in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and as a result the Canadian high commissioner was instructed to inform the South African government that the arrest and detention of Mr. Phillips could not but add to the widespread


public indignation already felt in Canada at the measures which had given rise to recent violence and loss of life in South Africa.
Those representations were made by the Canadian high commissioner in South Africa to the minister of external affairs of that country. Perhaps I might point out that as a result of those representations Mr. Phillips was released; an act which brought comment in the British House of Commons to the effect that the Canadian government seemed to have a good deal more ability to get Canadian newsmen released than was the case with the British government in its dealings concerning their newsmen who were in difficulties.
These steps have been taken; these protests have been made, and yet three days ago the national leader of the C.C.F., Mr. M. J. Coldwell, for whom we all have the greatest respect, is reported as stating this in Vancouver:
We've heard so much about human rights and fundamental freedoms from our present Prime Minister.
Yet when these human rights and fundamental freedoms are being fought for and people are being put to death in the fight for them, all we have from our present Prime Minister and our government in Ottawa is silence.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this statement was far from fair; it was completely inaccurate and misleading and could only have one effect, namely to stir up the Canadian people unjustly and try to convince them that their Prime Minister and their government did not care at all about what was happening in South Africa, and had cared so little that nothing whatever had been done to try to remedy the situation.
I do not mind criticism at all, but I ask hon. members with respect to the stand taken by Mr. Coldwell, what would they have the Canadian government do? What more could we have done short of withdrawing our high commissioner from South Africa, and would that have been the slightest bit of help in getting this very difficult problem solved?
It might be wise to consider the attitude taken by Mr. Hammerskjold, the Secretary General of the United Nations, and a great world statesman. As you know, Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago the security council passed a resolution which condemned the Union of South Africa. Mr. Hammarskjold, of course, then had the responsibility for doing something about the resolution but he did not run around the world making statements which could only incite people. In his effective way he has been able to arrange to have a conference with the foreign minister of South

Africa, and possibly other ministers, in London on May 12; and, furthermore, to visit South Africa himself during the month of July.
I do suggest that a similar attitude might be adopted in Canada. Extreme views on this question or on any other difficult question never help very much, and surely this is not the Canadian way to carry on. It is not the Canadian way to go to extremes of one kind or another. The reputation we have among the nations of the world is a reputation for a cool-headed attitude, and not for rushing off after this mirage or after that mirage and getting all excited and making fantastic statements.
I turn again in this connection to the same speech made by Mr. Coldwell, and may I say that there is no one whom I dislike more having to criticize. According to press reports, he said at Vancouver in the same speech:
The British commonwealth would be better off without South Africa . . . Withdrawal of South Africa from the commonwealth of nations would relieve the commonwealth of a terrific embarrassment.
In answer I would cite a statement made by another socialist public man, Mr. Nash, the Prime Minister of New Zealand. He said on March 31:
There is no way to save a holocaust in South Africa except by quiet reasoned discussion.
The proper approach to this question was given again yesterday by Prime Minister Macmillan in the British House of Commons when he was being questioned on this subject. He said:
All these matters are very much in our minds, terribly in our minds.
Mind you, although we in Canada think this problem is serious it is infinitely more difficult for the British.
What we here have to try to do is to use this coming conference to make all the progress we can in these matters, to preserve the unity of the commonwealth, and to see how far, in the more intimate discussions that the prime ministers are able to have with each other, they can make some useful contribution to the problem. I would venture to ask members and the house as a whole to recognize the very heavy responsibility that lies on this country at the moment.
Then there was an interjection by Mr. Manuel, a Labour member, who said, "On the government". Mr. Macmillan went on to say:
And on this government, in trying to steer in this most complicated question a wise course which will lead not merely to our priding ourselves on taking some outward action for which we can take credit, but which will lead to useful results on the lines along which we all want to see progress made.
These remarks, I suggest, set a very good standard for the discussions which will be taking place next week. It is worthy of note,
27. 1960	3327
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth Mr. Speaker, that even in South Africa there have been some hopeful developments. For example, the acting president of the cabinet, the Hon. Paul Sauer, said on April 19:
We must create a new spirit which must restore overseas faith-both white and non-white-in South Africa.
That is a statement by the man who happens to be leading the South African government at the present time.
I believe it is a very fortunate thing that there is going to be a commonwealth conference at this particular time. The problems that face any such conference are difficult but I do not believe that a more difficult problem has ever had to be faced by the prime ministers of the commonwealth than the particular one we are debating today.
Canada is not in the position of being without influence in the commonwealth. Canada is in a key position. Our attachment to the commonwealth goes very deep. It is probably the strongest attachment held by the Canadian people. Here we have an organization of ten nations, with more coming in all the time. Nigeria will be the eleventh nation on October 1 and will come into the commonwealth club of its own free will because it wants to be a member of the commonwealth.
A few weeks ago Mr. Nyerere, the leader of the main party in Tanganyika, was in Ottawa. It is a party, by the way, which is composed not only of African natives but of the white and Asiatic settlers in that country. He said here on more than one occasion that when his country gets its independence-they hope to get self-government this fall although perhaps not independence for a year or two-they intend to ask for membership in the commonwealth. He said that there are two organizations to which they want to belong, one being the United Nations and the other the commonwealth. He said that the commonwealth only exists as a matter of friendship and for mutual help and that even the communists never complain about it. He said that they cannot complain because there is nothing they can find wrong with the commonwealth.
Here we have this commonwealth, a bridge between all of the continents, under the leadership of the British and with the help of the other members, launching new nations in a way which is not being done anywhere else in the world. It is true that France is now following this example but the British have set the pace in an admirable way in launching new nations. That process is only nicely begun. There will be more and more such nations as time goes on.
It would be a world disaster if the commonwealth were allowed to break up, but if
3328	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth the extremists in Canada had their way and our Prime Minister and the other prime ministers went to London determined to make harsh statements and to demand violent action, how long does anyone in this chamber today think the commonwealth would last? This fact is recognized by the members of the commonwealth who have joined it since the second world war, by India, Pakistan, Ceylon, Ghana and Malaya. The statements made by the leaders of these countries on this very question, which touches them far more deeply than it does us and is far more serious for them, on the whole have been very restrained.
I suggest that we send our own Prime Minister to this conference next week with the feeling that the House of Commons and the Canadian people have confidence in him to do his part to work out this difficult problem.
These nine prime ministers and the foreign minister of South Africa-it is unfortunate that their prime minister cannot attend because of his disability-have the responsibility of dealing with this problem in such a way that progress is made toward the objective we have in mind of removing discrimination and of making certain that the commonwealth takes the right turn at this critical time in its history.
It can go on from now to make a far greater contribution in world affairs than it has ever made previously if good leadership is given during the next few days. May I suggest that we need have no fear about the future of the commonwealth being in safe hands at this conference in London.

This morning, Mr. Speaker, I was reading the Inaugural handbook of the Canadian national commission for UNESCO, I sholud like to introduce my remarks by two references from that handbook which is one of our own publications. On the first page, all by itself, I notice these words:
Peace, like happiness, Is a by-product of efforts directed to other proper ends; and the great advantage of concentration on immediate and worthy ends is that men of good will of all creeds and philosophies can join in them heartily.
Then on page 5 of this Inaugural Handbook I find the short, pithy opening speech that was given at the first conference of the Canadian national commission by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) of our country. He had this to say, and I quote from page 5:
I saw something of the beginnings of the United Nations in San Francisco in 1945. I saw there the great dedication of the nations to the principles of peace in the world and to the achievement of a reasonable equality of economic and cultural opportunity in every part of the world.


We could not agree more with the two excerpts I have quoted from this handbook of our Canadian national commission. It is on the precepts of those two quotations that I want to make my remarks this afternoon. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that if time only permitted, every member of our C.C.F. group in this house would like to speak on this matter because we feel so deeply concerned about the situation and what it can mean, if allowed to develop, to the future prosperity and peace of the world.
We in the C.C.F. sincerely hope that as a result of our discussions this afternoon a message will come from this House of Commons appealing to all Europeans in South Africa to recognize the insanity of apartheid and the need to come to terms with the situation by being prepared to negotiate with the African leaders and not to jail them. We feel that we are expressing the opinion of the vast majority of the Canadian people in asking, through the medium of what we say today in this House of Commons, the Europeans in South Africa to come to terms with the situation before it is too late and not to continue with an unsound approach, one which is tantamount to dictatorship, in an attempt to suppress 11 million people because, in so doing, they are not only inviting disaster, in our estimation, but are inviting widespread violence.
We in this group feel strongly a deep sense of shock because of the ruthless and murderous use of armed force in South Africa in order to compel obedience of the native Africans to what can only be termed cruel and unjust laws as exemplified by the apartheid policy. It is now evident-or it should be-that the suppression of every form of opposition in South Africa is being carried out-and apparently is so intended-with force of arms without regard to the grave possibilities of still further loss of life in that country.
I feel certain that all of us in this House of Commons and all the people of Canada condemn the apartheid policy or one of any degree of racial separateness-I believe that is one of the other terms that is used-because it can only mean inhuman treatment of the native Africans. The apartheid policy is based-whether or not they will agree to it in South Africa I do not know-on the master race philosophy. That philosophy was repudiated by western civilization in the last world war and certainly it was repudiated in the establishment of the universal declaration of human rights.
The policy we are now discussing and with which we are so seriously concerned is not only villainous but is perilous in that it denies

to at least 10 million people in South Africa elementary freedoms and rights of citizenship in order to maintain the rule of the whites in South Africa. If my reading is correct, Mr. Speaker, more than half of the entire white population of the African continent is in South Africa; but in South Africa the whites are outnumbered by more than four to one. It therefore surely follows that the apartheid policy cannot be made to work without poisoning the whole continent of Africa and without causing a violent upheaval which, indications would lead us to believe, could endanger the whole world.
It is because of our feelings in this regard that we call upon, request and plead with the Prime Minister of Canada to raise this issue when he attends the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London. We ask that the horror over recent events as felt by the Canadian people be fully expressed by the Prime Minister when he is at that conference. We feel certain that definite and pungent analysis and expression of our feelings on this matter by the Prime Minister will encourage those in South Africa who oppose the government's merciless and dictatorship policy.
At the same time may I on behalf of this group say that we also urge support of any action by the United Nations to mobilize world public opinion on the side of sanity and humanitarian principles in a stern reproof to the South African government. May we also add that we urge upon the Prime Minister and the Canadian government to offer as a humanitarian gesture an emergency measure to grant political asylum in Canada to the refugees from South Africa.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) spoke much of the British commonwealth of nations, and Canada of course is an important part of the commonwealth of nations. But I am afraid that it is not generally recognized that this British commonwealth of nations, of which we are so proud to be a part, is composed of a majority of nations the people of which have a skin pigment which is not white. The last census of which I have taken note gives a total population in the British commonwealth of nations of 629 million. Of that 629 million 500 million are non-white. Therefore, when the Secretary of State for External Affairs comes out with the exhortation which he did and the enthusiasm which he did- and I noticed the ceremony with which he did it-when a few moments ago he said what a world calamity it would be if the British commonwealth broke up, he should remember that 500 million of this 629 million in the British commonwealth are nonwhite.
27, 1960	3329
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth
This means that if you want to hold the British commonwealth together you have to hold together those countries which are nonwhite and which today are waiting very carefully what is taking place in South Africa, the policy of South Africa, and the attitude of the countries which are white in the British commonwealth toward the apartheid policy and the violence, dictatorship and suppression of freedoms which has resulted.
It would be logical and reasonable that those countries should look to us to find out whether democracy has a real and fundamental meaning. I believe I made mention when I spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne of the marvellous opportunity granted to yourself, myself and four others to go to Australia for the biennial conference of the commonwealth parliamentary association, where we met with the non-white members of the commonwealth; where we heard how they were disturbed at the discrimination between races and colours; where we heard of their disturbance at the policy of South Africa; and where we heard from everyone how they looked to Canada to give leadership, to take definite stands and to make its voice known and heard.
On analysis it is understandable that there are reactions and objections by the people of South Africa to what is taking place there under the policy of apartheid. From my own reading I was amazed to find that in a so-called democratic country of this world, a member of the British commonwealth, they have a pass system. And of course it is the pass system to which the African people look with abhorrence, recognizing it as a badge of absolute subjection. I think I am not far wrong when I say that it is against that pass system that the South Africans have been particularly demonstrating in the past few weeks. I gather from what I have been able to read that every African of the age of 16 years and over must hold a pass. Without that pass he cannot move into towns; he cannot obtain employment; and indeed, without that pass he is denied all freedom. If he is discovered without a pass he suffers a fine or imprisonment.
If that were not enough in a free country of the British commonwealth, look at the land system. It is a land system which discriminates against the African population. Less than 15 per cent of the land area in the Union of South Africa is allocated to three quarters of the population which is African. Over 85 per cent is allocated to the white minority of three million, and no African can hold freehold land anywhere in the Union of South Africa, even on the South African Bantu reserves.
3330	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth
It is a situation like that which causes us to view the position of the native Africans in South Africa in relation to the policy of apartheid of that government. The Prime Minister of Great Britain has been mentioned several times this afternoon by both the previous speakers. We have to admire the courage with which he spoke in South Africa and admire certain actions which have been taken since his return to the United Kingdom. We noted with interest an eloquent phrase which he used when he spoke in Capetown. He referred to the "winds of change". That is a very eloquent phrase. Africans in all Africa are feeling the winds of change, and this in South Africa no different from anywhere else.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned, in some parts of the African continent the winds are blowing almost like a hurricane. They are blowing through Nigeria, which is going to become independent very shortly. They are blowing through the Belgian Congo, which is going to become completely independent on July 1. It is certainly understandable that the Africans in South Africa want the same rights and liberties as their brothers and cousins elsewhere on the continent and elsewhere in the British commonwealth of nations.
A great deal has been said by myself and the previous speakers about the British commonwealth of nations. Surely the basic principle of our commonwealth is the maintenance and furtherance of human rights and fundamental freedoms. One could wax very emotional about the commonwealth, but I think that fundamentally the maintenance and furtherance of human rights and fundamental freedoms is the basic reason for the continued existence of our commonwealth. If we believe that, then we in Canada have the responsibility to demonstrate by our speeches and our action this afternoon that we firmly believe that the commonwealth has a constructive purpose, namely to insist that the United Nations declaration of human rights is more than wishful thinking, and that it is of concern to us in Canada as a partner in the British commonwealth of nations.
We are very happy that the opportunity has been granted for this discussion to take place this afternoon. We are bitterly disappointed that the procedure is such that all one can do is talk, and that all the Prime Minister can take to the prime ministers' conference in London is an expression of individual opinions as they are given here today. Very often we hear of the leadership given by the United Kingdom; of the true meaning of the mother of parliaments and


of the courage and devotion of the British. I wish the procedure this afternoon in this Canadian House of Commons had been such that the Prime Minister of Canada when he leaves tomorrow could take with him a motion unanimously expressing the views of all members of this house as to what they think of the apartheid policies of South Africa and how dangerous they could be to the future of the commonwealth and to the peace of the world. Surely, if the House of Commons in Great Britain could do it, why can we not do the same?
I was most interested to read the motion which was passed unanimously in the United Kingdom House of Commons on Friday, April 8 of this year. It is to be found in their Hansard report at page 775. This is what the people's representatives in all parties in the United Kingdom House of Commons had to say; this is the motion which was carried, and I quote:
That this house, deploring the present racialist policies now being pursued by the South African government, under which non-Europeans are consistently denied normal human and political rights, including the right of campaigning for a peaceful change in the laws under which they live, and the recent declaration of a state of emergency and the many arbitrary arrests, fearing that a continuation of this repression is threatening the security and welfare of all races living in the Union of South Africa and good relations between members of the commonwealth, urges-
I wish I had the right to insert, here, the name of the Prime Minister of Canada.
-the prime minister to take the opportunity at the forthcoming commonwealth prime ministers' conference to bring home to the South African government the strong feelings of the British people on this question; and states its firm belief that peace and tranquility in South Africa can only be secured on the basis of freedom and equality and a full respect for the inherent dignity and humanity of all men.
That was the motion which was passed unanimously in the United Kingdom. Thus, the prime minister of Great Britain could convey not only the sentiments contained in a number of speeches; he could convey to the conference the unanimous opinion of the people's representatives on the subject of apartheid in its relation to the world and to all the partners in the commonwealth.
If the procedure of this house had permitted I would most certainly have moved a resolution identical with that which was carried in the United Kingdom House of Commons, changing the words only where necessary so as to read "the Prime Minister of Canada" instead of "the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom", and "the people of Canada" for "the people of Britain".
Having heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of the government, having heard from the Leader of the

Opposition on behalf of the Liberal party, and having heard the views of the C.C.F., it is clear that we are without doubt unanimous in our views on this vital question, and because of that, and because we wish to help the Prime Minister and to strengthen his hand with regard to this humanitarian and far-reaching question, I should like to ask whether the Prime Minister himself would not give consideration to asking for the unanimous consent of the house-because by unanimous consent all procedure and standing orders can be changed-to permit the introduction of a resolution along the lines which I have suggested which, as I said, is word for word the same as that already agreed to in Great Britain.
To say anything more would be repetitious. I wish to conclude, having made a reference to the House of Commons in the United Kingdom, by reading the last statement made before the vote was taken as it appears at page 848 of the British Hansard:
I know that all the people of South Africa will not hear all of it because their newspapers are censured, but I hope they will hear enough to realize that the House of Commons feels very strongly that it is our duty not to keep silent but to do all we can to help our friends in South Africa to help themselves and to put an end to this terrible tragedy which has overcome their land.
To that, we say "amen".

I am
pleased to have the opportunity to take part in this discussion which is of such interest to us all. The discussion of such a subject marks, it seems to me, the growing maturity of Canada inasmuch as we are devoting our attention to the outside world and to the consideration of our place and role therein. It is such a short time ago in the history of our nation that a discussion of any aspect of foreign policy was very rare indeed.
I should like to join the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in his words of good wishes to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) as he leaves for the commonwealth prime ministers' conference, and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) as he goes to Europe to take part in very important international gatherings. I am sure all of us will keep them in our thoughts as they participate in these vital deliberations on behalf of world peace.
I think it is fitting that the motion of the Leader of the Opposition should embrace this matter within the framework of commonwealth considerations. He is quite right, and I was interested in his remarks about the development of the commonwealth, that unique political institution which seems capable of such great diversity and variety while at the same time retaining the fundamental values which have made it one of the

It is significant, too, that today we are giving our attention to the great continent of Africa, surely the continent of the future. So often we used to refer to Africa as the dark continent and perhaps in many ways it was, although, as has been said by Professor Kimble, it is perhaps true that the darkest thing about Africa was our own ignorance of it. Such ignorance and lack of concern can no longer prevail because today we must consider this great new area that is seeing the emergence of great new nations dealing so importantly in world affairs.
It has been said that the struggle in Africa has not been and is not only for self-government, but for self-respect. We have watched that development and of course Canada is tremendously interested in it because in Africa there are and there will be political and social developments of vital concern. One is perhaps led to think of the ancient parable spoken about putting old wine in new bottles as one looks at some of the sociological, political and economic developments in this great continent which are occasionally disturbing.
The subject of apartheid is of widespread interest today. We read a great deal about it in the press but one cannot help observe that matters of interest to the press are not necessarily equated with matters of importance. But beyond the press and radio and television this is a question being discussed by legislatures and by citizens. Surely all of us are as one in our concern for the human suffering which is taking place in the Union of South Africa. There is surely no monopoly of concern or regard for severe violations of the sanctity of the human personality. Of course, the difficulties have not taken place only in the last few days. There have been problems aplenty in that area of the world for a long time. There are many grave and serious difficulties there and there will be more. Lord Balfour said that in South Africa a white nation has established itself in a black continent and that is something that has never before presented itself in the history of mankind. It is not surprising that some of the problems of that nation are unique and dreadful in their complexity.
We can all share our concern for the future in Africa if certain policies are pursued and if adjustments, accommodations and re-thinking do not take place along certain lines. It would be very easy for any hon. member of

Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth this parliament-I think I could do it although it is not my nature-to denounce and make inflammatory speeches about what is going on in the Union of South Africa. It was Milton who said it is always easier to be critical than correct. There are some Canadians who say, "Throw South Africa out of the commonwealth." That is a favourite expression. There are some who seem as anxious to have South Africa thrown out of the commonwealth as they are to have red China brought into the United Nations. But are these suggestions in the best interests? Are these the wisest policies to follow?
In his usual wisdom I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs expressed it well when he said that these extreme measures are not the Canadian way. I do not feel called upon to utter inflammatory, condemnatory statements. I do not think that at this juncture they are necessary or helpful.
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs was quite right when he said that Canada need not go to these extremes to make clear its attitude and point of view. I am sure there is no doubt anywhere in the world as to where Canada stands on the matter of human rights.
I had the privilege to represent my country in one of the committees of the United Nations and for three years had an opportunity to deal in a minor way-and I would not pretend it was otherwise-with delegates from all over the world, from the United Nations and its 82 members. I never found any doubt as to where Canada stood on these matters. There is no question about the liberality of Canada's views in the world scene. Certainly there is no question as to the prevailing attitude of the Prime Minister. I first heard of the man who is now Prime Minister of Canada not in connection with a matter of politics but in connection with his advocacy for certain aspects of human rights and fundamental freedoms to which he has been devoted all his life. It is axiomatic to say he is a great defender of human freedoms. That is known not only throughout this land but throughout the world.
Would we be rendering our best services to mankind in pillorying the government of another nation or castigating its laws, no matter how repugnant those laws are to our thinking and no matter to what extent we may feel they lack something in inward wisdom? For the Canadian House of Commons and those of us who are its members to spend time publicly denouncing the laws of another country strikes in me a minor chord of unease. I wonder what other countries there are in the world upon whose laws and actions


we might sincerely pass critical judgment? Are there not other areas on the earth's surface where the human personality is being violated? I submit that if it were not for certain aspects of freedom we would not know what was going on in the Union of South Africa. The things which emerge from certain other parts of the world represent a far greater degradation of the human personality than what emerges from the Union of South Africa. This is not to be construed in any way as an effort to condone, pass over or diminish the importance of these events which we deplore, but I cannot support as a matter of policy and of function the Canadian parliament and people devoting themselves to this purpose.
There is another aspect of the case that causes me no small feeling of concern. I believe the Leader of the Opposition referred to this in his address to which I listened with the greatest interest. There is the danger of moral priggishness in taking such a course. I would want to avoid any self-righteousness in this regard. It was said that he who is without sin should cast the first stone. I think it behooves us to think very carefully about this, examine the question closely and make sure that as individuals and members of groups we are at all times making the maximum effort to fulfil and develop our beliefs in the fundamental freedoms, in the equality of man and in our repudiation of anything which even approaches racial intolerance or prejudice. Canada has a very fine record in this respect but there are some things in which the area for improvement is fairly significant.
But I think the major consideration of all is again, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs expressed it, that the moderate course is the better course. There are still some moderates in the Union of South Africa; there are still men of liberal mind- I would have to write that liberal with a small "1", of course-and there are still areas for moderation.
If I thought that a bitter denunciation, an inflammatory attack upon this state; if I thought that working up Canadian public opinion to be blistering in its denunciation; if I thought that a blistering denunciation in a group to which I do not belong, namely the commonwealth prime ministers' conference, was helpful, I could easily recommend such a course. We can denounce, we can criticize, but in so doing would we by our act be helping the people of the Union of South Africa who now most need our help in the difficult and trying times which are so much on our minds.

I think of the need of dealing with the great problem of the area of southwest Africa, where the Union of South Africa has a responsibility before the world as a mandatory power from the league of nations. I can recall when this question was before the United Nations. I remember the bitter denunciations and the part of the world from which they sometimes came. I saw that over the last few years there were opportunities for some rapprochement, for some process of negotiation, to which the union would be a part. I thought then how wise and sound it was not to close irrevocably the door for discussion, for negotiation, upon which is based the future hopes for improvement of those people.
The Prime Minister of Great Britain has been referred to by every speaker today. I had the privilege of sitting in the gallery of the British House of Commons some time ago when the Prime Minister of Great Britain was being asked-as was the Prime Minister of our own country-about the very question we have now before us. I was so impressed by the wisdom of his reply. He said:
Of course, what has happened in this tragic situation is a very great source of deep regret to me.
I share to the full the feelings of sympathy for those who have suffered, but I ask the house to consider our position not as a party matter. The British commonwealth has, I think, a great past.
I believe it to have the possibilities of a great future. It will outlast the particular people who preside over the fortunes of any country at any given time.
I think that we must remember not lightly to throw away or to injure what I am certain in the years ahead will be a great instrument for good.
Then he went on to talk about the heavy responsibility which rested upon the government and perhaps especially upon him. He said:
I think it has been made clear already that the agenda of the formal conferences is fixed by the conference itself. There are certain traditions about it.
He expressed the hope that the Prime Minister of the Union of South Africa would be there and he went on to say that the course which was suggested to him was quite different from taking an action which would precipitate a crisis in the commonwealth. He continued:
Britain has a great responsibility here, and what I want to do is to use the commonwealth and see it grow, but so to steer a course that we are able to preserve in full the structure which has been built up and to see that we do not err in precipitate action which might have very dangerous results.
He then went on to say:
I have expressed my view privately, and in a courteous way, as I thought, and I have tried to do so publicly. Our duty is to influence and to guide and to hope that, by so doing, the principles in which we believe will be accepted everywhere. But I repeat-and I think the right hon. gentleman

knows the position that he would be in if he had the same responsibility-that we have to be bold in the statement of our views but cautious in any action which, foolishly carried out, might jeopardize the whole structure of our commonwealth proceedings in their formal character.
I commend this particular reference to the hon. member from the C.C.F. who has just spoken. I see no members of that group in the house at the present time. I commend to them this wise and reasoned statement of the Prime Minister of Great Britain but I do not rest my case and I do not rest my concern only on the remarks of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. Knowing the record of our own Prime Minister and his wisdom, knowing what the commonwealth has been and will be, I am sure that the counsel of moderation and of reason will prevail.
I have no doubt, and I am sure the Canadian people have no doubt, that we can trust our leaders on this very moot issue that is before us. I know that in the discussion of it in high places our Prime Minister and Canada will play the highest part; I know that Canada will be found to be on the side of freedom and a supporter of justice and a proponent of reason and a purveyor of wisdom. On these grounds I feel that this most delicate issue will be dealt with by our Prime Minister and his colleagues.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened closely to the four members who took part in this important debate, I should like at this time to associate myself with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) not only in the splendid speech he has delivered but also with regard to the principles he has stated on behalf of the party to which I have the honour to belong.
The statement he made in this house is one against the policy of apartheid, of discrimination, of segregation, not against a minority, but against a majority which has been discriminated against on account of its race and of its colour.
Mr. Speaker, we, who are sitting on this side of the house, believe that all men are equal before God. We believe that all men were created in his image and resemblance. We also believe that the Creator considers them as such, on an equal footing, and if some men on earth happen to be of a certain colour or to belong to a certain race, or to profess a certain religion, while others belong to a people of another race, of another colour, or to practice another religion, we must recognize that this is an accident beyond the control of those men.
3334	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth
The United Nations, as the Leader ol the Opposition ably pointed out, have condemned in principle racial persecution, but were reluctant to go any further, fearing they would violate the doctrine of sovereignty, fearing to intervene too deeply in the domestic and national problem of individual nations.
By virtue of the principle whereby nations should not interfere in the affairs of others, it becomes very important for other nations of the world to know whether that principle does not also affect their personal business or their own position, or whether that principle might not have serious repercussions on other countries of the world. And should it become necessary to intervene in the affairs of another country-and I think that is a distinct possibility in this case-even if only by a resolution of the house or by a statement of opinion such as we have heard from the four hon. members who spoke before me, I think it then becomes important, indeed necessary, to take a stand on a state of affairs which exists in another country and may well have repercussions in Canada.
I think, therefore Mr. Speaker, that we must condemn this policy of apartheid. We must do so because it is a bad policy, a wrong one, and because it is contrary to human rights, to justice, to morality and to natural law.
I wonder how far I can go along with the attitude displayed a moment ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). Personally, I have some doubts as to whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs was entirely right in the statement he made. Oh, I do not say that we should not do all we can to maintain the unity of the British commonwealth of nations, but I wonder if, when that unity is threatened because one of the members of the commonwealth is persecuting a majority, whether the unity of the commonwealth is still easy to maintain.
Unfortunately, the history of minorities throughout the world does not always make palatable reading.
In Canada, our own minority has not always enjoyed equal and fair treatment. This is less true because history, experience, the passage of years and particularly the thinking of a large number of those who make up Canada's majority have taught most Canadians that there was no longer any excuse for such a situation.
I also think we should thank Providence that Canada does not have problems similar to those now prevailing in South Africa.


That is why, coming back to the main theme of the debate, I insist that we, in the opposition, strongly protest against the apartheid policy under which human beings are being persecuted because of their race and colour, and justice is being trampled under foot as if it did not exist for coloured people.
We are concerned about the disastrous consequences of that policy which recently has led to the arbitrary arrest of individuals and their detention without a hearing; a policy which has led to violence, unfortunate killings and bloodshed.
It is a policy that must cease if normal relations are to be restored in that country of the British commonwealth of nations. Peace, order and security cannot exist without due respect for the individual.
Like the previous speakers, may I urge the Prime Minister to take note of the views expressed on both sides of the house and particularly of the suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition who has a wide experience, not only in the United Nations, but in many other places, and to make his views known at the conference he will be attending shortly. We wish him every success. We know very well that his parliamentary experience will help him to remember not only what took place here, but what is taking place at present in Canada, and the anxiety that grips the population in various quarters in this country on account of recent happenings in South Africa. We trust he will also remember the fear and anxiety that is felt in all civilized countries of the world.
On the strength of those arguments and of those views, if not of the resolutions which have been put on record, the Prime Minister will be able to make known with greater justice and greater force the views which, I am sure, he himself intended to express to his colleagues of the British commonwealth countries.
