speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members in the house this afternoon were impressed by the unanimity of viewpoint, as one might expect among members on both sides of the house, with regard to this very important matter.
My first words must be of thanks and appreciation to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for the manner in which he presented the viewpoint not only of the opposition but, in general, of hon. members of this house. May I say to him that the restraint with which he spoke was in keeping with what I would expect from one who- whatever our differences of opinion may be,

and sometimes they are very strongly and definitely expressed-is regarded by me and I know by members in the house generally as having made a worth-while contribution to external affairs in this country. He has won for himself the Nobel prize for peace and all of us join in a realization of its importance. I say that because today the House of Commons was at its best. Indeed there was that feeling that here in this chamber all of us are in a cathedral of devotion to the abiding principles of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
I want to thank my friend and colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) for his words. After all, we in public life expect to be judged and often misjudged. However, I want to thank him for his words when he referred to the attitude I have taken through the years, when it was not always popular, on behalf of those things which represent more than life itself, namely the civil liberties of the individual.
On an occasion like this I might be allowed to look back in retrospect. I recall an occasion in 1922 when it was not popular in my province to take a stand on behalf of the rights of the other language in this country and when counsel were afraid that to take that position would be detrimental. That has been my attitude through the years, namely a belief in the need, at all costs, to preserve those things that represent the recognition of the sacredness of the human personality.
I am glad that the opportunity has come to say a few words on this subject which has actuated the minds of my fellow Canadians and indeed those of people in every part of the world in recent weeks. It is not a new matter. Apartheid has existed since 1948. Year in and year out it has come before the United Nations. I criticize no one today when I say that through the years Canada abstained because of the principle that interference in the domestic field of any nation was not a thing to be accepted by the United Nations.
I welcome the opportunity first because it enables the Secretary of State for External Affairs to place before the country the views of the government. But more particularly do I welcome the occasion in that it has provided an opportunity for the House of Commons to express its united viewpoint; for there are no frontiers or divisions between hon. members-whatever their location may be in the house-on the need for maintaining those freedoms without which mankind cannot rise to its full stature.
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth
Some mention was made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) of the fact that an opportunity should have been available for the moving of a motion; and he quoted with approval what had taken place in the British House of Commons. Let me point out that the motion in the British House of Commons was made as a private members' motion and resolution in an hour set aside for the discussion of private members' resolutions. I would also point out that during that day in question, namely April 8, there were several motions. There was one dealing with medical diseases which took from 11.05 to 12.32. The question was put and agreed to. Then came the motion of the hon. member for Wednesbury which was quoted by the hon. member.
There was no other way in which to bring this matter before the house than by the means adopted by the Leader of the Opposition today. I would point out this fact. When about two weeks ago I spoke on this subject and referred to the possibility of there being a debate, my natural view was that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), having regard to Monday being the last private members' day, would have permitted the clearing away of a number of cases on a subject that is receiving general attention from members of the C.C.F. party. If that had been so, we could have placed on private members' motions a motion similar to the one indicated by the hon. gentleman and with consent could have proceeded to discuss it. However, that course has been denied by the attitude taken on Monday last-the last private members' day-by the hon. gentleman's colleagues.
Having referred to that fact, may I say this. Having no disagreement on this matter and having heard the views of the house, we will all be reinforced in the sure knowledge that there are no divisions of opinion on this matter.
The Leader of the Opposition, with the experience that has been his, referred to the nature of the prime ministers' conferences, their composition, the informality that prevailed, and the freedom from any fixed determination in advance as to the course to be followed. Indeed, commonwealth prime ministers' conferences are most informal meetings. The various prime ministers sit about the table in the cabinet room at No. 10 Downing street. Then in that spirit, mystical as it is, which binds the members of the commonwealth together in frankness, but with that tolerance which must always prevail between members of a family, matters are discussed. Determinations are not made.
3336	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth Communiques issued at the end of the conference contain nothing upon which there is not complete and unanimous agreement.
The hon. member for Vancouver East mentioned the debate in the British house, and I refer to the words of the minister of state for commonwealth relations who discussed in general the meaning of these conferences. As reported on page 830 of the British Hansard, he said:
The secret of the success which has attended these conferences in the past, indeed the mystery- to use the word in its old English sense-of commonwealth relations lies in the informality of its methods combined with a respect for certain principles which, with the exception perhaps of the Statute of Westminster, are not contained in any formal document-
We must not forget that there are few commonwealth countries whose policies have not at some time or another aroused controversy in one or more of the others.
If a commonwealth prime ministers' conference became an occasion at which any prime minister might have the domestic policies of his government criticized and arraigned by his colleagues, I have little doubt that such conferences would cease to be acceptable to commonwealth prime ministers generally.
I mentioned that on an earlier occasion. There is no formula under which prime ministers meet. There is no record kept except an informal one. There are no motions made. Through the instrumentality of joint discussion comes a realization of the problems of each other.
I thank the Leader of the Opposition for the good wishes he expressed to me on this occasion and for his wish that a constructive conference will be the result. He dealt with the commonwealth at some length. He described its evolution; difficult to understand, impossible of definition. It has simply advanced not from precedent to precedent but from innovation to innovation. He asked the question whether or not the Canadian parliament had the right and the duty to intervene in matters of concern, particularly to one or other of the member nations. He pointed out, too, that wherever discrimination takes place it leads inevitably to disaster. We say that we cannot win a nuclear war, that no nation can win it. Equally so no nation today can win a race war within or without its territories.
Again quoting from British Hansard, the following appears at page 833. I am quoting the minister of state for commonwealth relations to whom I have already referred:
No one who has ... shared the hopes and expectations of seeing there-
He is referring to South Africa.
-the spread of order, tolerance and freedom can fail to be heart-broken by the events which have occurred there during these last weeks. The antidote is to seek the best way which lies within our power to help to set these things right, and to


prevent a situation arising in which South Africa finds itself in one of the cul-de-sacs of history from which there can be no escape except through violence and tragedy.
Mr. Speaker, that is the purpose of this discussion today, to reinforce me as the representative of this nation, having held these views throughout the years, with the conscience, thought and deliberation of the Canadian House of Commons in order to air the views which have been expressed on matters which are of particular moment at this time.
Through the years I have advocated in this house, although my view was not accepted, that nothing could be more helpful to a prime minister than a discussion of such matters, to the end that through discussion the prime ministers' conference may have presented to it the views of the Canadian people bodied in the thinking of the members both of the House of Commons and of the Senate as well as Canadians generally.
I have never quite felt the same after the trip I took a year and a half ago as to the meaning of the commonwealth. I was in the countries of the commonwealth in Asia, and whatever the colour, race or religion there was something intangible there which was beyond description. There was a feeling that never would it be possible for members of the commonwealth to be at war with one another regardless of their differences, however strong they may be. Wherever I went I visited the courts, and I felt that there the rule of law applied and that the common law, brought in line with local conditions, gave to us belonging to the commonwealth a bond. I believe that in the years ahead there will more and more come a realization that only through the assurance and the acceptance of the equality of man can there be that unity which will place the commonwealth, as it is becoming today, in the position of a bulwark against communism and everything it stands for.
That is why discrimination is dangerous. Communism marches not so much on empty stomachs and on poverty as it does on the fact that while all of us pay lip service to the equality of man and to the brotherhood of man without regard to race or colour, none of us is completely free from intolerance. Wherever there is discrimination-as the hon. member said referring to the meeting of the parliamentary association which he attended -there you have the beginnings of a situation which ultimately cannot but achieve a mobilization by the communists, who, whatever their tyranny may be, give every indication in their words of the equality of the individual.

As I prepare for the meeting which will begin next week in London it is of assistance to me to have heard the speeches which have been made today. This subject arouses profound emotions. It cannot but result in powerful expressions of opinion. It requires, however, as the Leader of the Opposition said, clarity of thinking coupled with responsibility. I could make a speech on this subject; it might be attractive for the moment, and it might receive widespread support, but if in dealing with the subject my contribution was not one which led to a solution of this problem but, actually, to its exacerbation, the wish to do so would be denied by the reality.
I do not intend to go over the attitude of the government to date. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has done so. He has referred to the representations made by the Canadian government and by himself to the representative of South Africa. On April 9, in a statement which has been subject to criticism, I spoke of Canada's indignation at what was happening. The work of responsible statesmanship today is not to arouse, is not to please, is not to mobilize the plaudits of the moment. Otherwise instead of bringing about a solution of the problem or an atmosphere in which the problem can be solved, what we do is add to the fires. Our responsibility everywhere within the commonwealth is to make the commonwealth a bridge based on tolerance which will bring to the white, the black and all the other colours that are represented in this commonwealth, equality through moderation. Discretion in discussion does not mean acquiescence, or toleration of the thing with which we disagree.
Mr. Speaker, no Canadian views this policy as being right or workable. What shall we do in order to bring about before it is too late a realization that discrimination wherever practised is a forerunner, first of tyranny and then of ultimate change by force, bloodshed and discord? We recognize the complexity of the problem of racial relations. As I said a moment ago, no country can claim to have a perfect record in this field. Where were we in the days of war and after the war? I criticize no one, but I recall on one occasion speaking when the Japanese, because of their race and for no other reason -not the crime they had committed or which it was anticipated they would commit-could be banished from Canada. None of us can speak without sin on this subject. We have gone a long way along the road toward solving this problem. An organization of coloured people in Toronto-and I wish I had its name here-has made representations to me which I can only commend for their sanity,
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth their reason and their responsibility. This organization realizes that much remains to be done, that the steps forward toward national or international tolerance are slow. We realize that, but at the same time we recognize that repression as a deterrent to progress toward racial equality can never be accepted.
I share in full the feelings of those both within and outside this house who have emphasized their hatred of policies of discrimination. Such policies can only lead to the negation of human rights. All of us, whether we can express our views or not, feel a deep sense of outrage at those things wherever they may be, which constitute a denial of the sacredness of human personality.
What about the situation? The Secretary of State for External Affairs asked the question: what should we have done? We made our views clear. Noising views from the house tops is not always a safe method in matters such as this, indeed in any deliberations or in any phase of life in which you try to secure through arguments the attainment of your objective.
Some say, "What have we done?" My answer is: What of the other nations of the commonwealth? Mention was made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs of the text of the resolution at the United Nations. That resolution constituted a major step forward toward the achievement of international tolerance. Nine nations voted for it. Great Britain and France abstained not because they loved apartheid but because the circumstances were such that they felt that this constituted an interference by the United Nations in domestic affairs which in itself would result in a veto on any action being taken. This resolution represented the conscience of mankind. The text of the resolution is as follows:
The security council, having considered the complaint oi 29 member states concerning the situation arising out of the large-scale killings of unarmed and peaceful demonstrators against racial discrimination and segregation in the Union of South Africa.
Recognizing that such a situation has been brought about by the racial policies of the government of the Union of South Africa and the continued disregard by that government of the resolutions of the general assembly calling upon it to revise its policies and bring them into conformity with its obligations and responsibilities under the charter.
Taking into account the strong feelings and grave concern aroused among governments and peoples of the world by the happenings in the Union South Africa.
1.	Recognizes that the situation in the Union of South Africa is one that has led to international friction and if continued might endanger international peace and security.
2.	Deplores that the recent disturbances in the Union of South Africa should have led to the loss of life of so many Africans and extends to the families of the victims its deepest sympathies.
3338	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth
3.	Deplores the policies and actions of the government of the Union of South Africa which have given rise to the present situation.
4.	Calls upon the government of the Union of South Africa to initiate measures aimed at bringing about racial harmony based on equality in order to ensure that the present situation does not continue or recur and to abandon its policies of apartheid and racial discrimination.
5.	Requests the secretary general, in consultation with the government of the Union of South Africa, to make such arrangements as would adequately help in upholding the purposes and principles of the charter and to report to the security council whenever necessary and appropriate.
That resolution was brought about in advance. The secretary general, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, will meet the representative of South Africa in London at the prime ministers' conference on May 12. Later on, the secretary general will be going to South Africa. A major step forward has been achieved.
What of the attitude of the British on this resolution? Whatever we would say of them, they have a knowledge of diplomacy and of international rights. The foreign secretary said-and I paraphrase-that he was afraid the resolution would only make the South African government more stubborn. However, as things have turned out there has been a very long stride forward as a result of international action.
What of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom? We hear criticism as to what we should do. It is suggested that the government should seek to bring about South Africa's expulsion or exclusion from the commonwealth. I will refer to that in a moment. That statement was recently made by several, including the hon. member for Assiniboia, if reported correctly and in his absence I repeat, if reported correctly. It is also suggested that strong formal protests should be addressed to the South African government. That is the second general suggestion. The third is that at the meeting next week of the prime ministers there should be on the part of the leaders of the commonwealth countries other than South Africa a strong collective and public expression of condemnation or disapproval of the South African policy.
Let us see what the attitude is of those who have responsibility. What did Mr. Macmillan say? The Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned what he had said yesterday. This matter-as I paraphrase what he said-will not be on the agenda formally. Mr. Speaker, can you believe that each of us outside the Union of South Africa will not make clear, informally, our views? Can you see them sitting around that table without informally making known their views? India, Mr. Nehru; Pakistan, General Ayub Khan;
[Mr. Diefenbaker.J

Ceylon-well, they have started another election so I do not know who will represent them-Malaya. Mr. Macmillan already has said yesterday what he would do.
What about Mr. Menzies? Mr Menzies has been in office in Australia longer than any prime minister in the history of that country. That wise statesman said:
Prime ministers' conferences do not have matters listed for discussion. They do not have an agenda. They do not have votes taken. They do not have majorities.
When some people tell me I should bring this up and have a vote, I invite them to consider what would happen if there were a vote in a prime ministers' conference. Suppose someone moved to throw Canada out saying we did something that the others disliked. Suppose someone disliked our policies with reference to the migration of peoples. If we were to start having motions and majorities in prime ministers' conferences it would not be very long before all of us would have voted the rest out. There is no question about that. But it is easy for some who write editorials to say what should be done.
The Leader of the Opposition today-and I again express my views respecting his speech -spoke with the authority and knowledge that experience assures.

speechtext:
Making due allowance for the wording which still expresses my idea, Mr. Menzies said this:
They consist of, say, nine people sitting together each of them the head of the government of his own country, discussing matters of common interest informing each other's minds, learning from each other's experience, getting to know something more about the problems of other men. These are not meetings where votes are taken. Indeed, I should like to tell hon. members that even the communique which emerges at the end of a commonwealth prime ministers' conference-and it is always a harmless enough document, as you know-cannot contain anything to the inclusion of which even only one prime minister objects.
Then, he goes on:
The opposition says: "Put it down on the agenda."
How often have I read that in the last few days as coming from those who have no responsibility. I continue:
Put it down on the agenda. Bring along the prime minister of South Africa. Let him be put into the dock and let us all try to cross-examine him. How long does anybody suppose the commonwealth would last if that was the way we went on?
When I read what the pundits say I wonder whether they have read what Mr. Nehru said.

He tabled a resolution in the Indian parliament. It deplored the incidents and sent sympathy to the Africans who had suffered from the firing and from the policy of racial discrimination and the suppression of the African people in their own homeland. He said, "This is a moral issue." There was no question raised by him that he intends to formalize his feelings.
When we hear my friends of the socialist party saying what they would do if they were here I ask them to read what Prime Minister Nash had to say on the subject. I have his statement here which is dated March 31. Prime Minister Nash has not made a request that the South African racial policy be discussed in the commonwealth prime ministers' conference. His words are these:
I have, in fact, repeatedly emphasized that internal affairs of commonwealth countries of a controversial nature are not normally discussed at prime ministers' conferences. If they were-and the inclusion of South Africa's racial policies would be a matter for Dr. Verwoerd-I should make whatever contribution I could in a common endeavour to find a solution to the existing grave situation in South Africa.
Then later he was asked on April 11 about New Zealand's attitude toward the South African question. He replied it was a matter of record that he did not think there were any racially superior people. Then he added these words, that he would not say anything to make things worse than they are. Then he went on to say:
Unless some super statesmanship was used by someone there might be a worse condition than has yet been known in the conflict between the races.
What about Ceylon? Ceylon's feelings were expressed by the representative at the U.N. council, when he strongly criticized the policies of the South African government as ugly and almost indecent. The prime minister of Ceylon expressed his aversion to any form of racial discrimination and felt the security council resolution carried more weight than if countries took up the matter individually. These are the prime ministers who are going to meet; these are prime ministers of another colour who have felt the horrors of discrimination and condemn it. But the pundits say, "Speak up." And do what? Speak up in public and do what?
At the present time I share the feelings of those who have expressed themselves strongly. I am not going to repeat what I have said in the past. Some of them, if they were standing here, would realize that however attractive outspoken criticism may be, we should speak only in a moderate but direct, clear and frank expression of views not in the open market, which, according to many, has made South Africa stubborn, but to the individual who represents that country.

Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth
In the few moments remaining I am going to deal with some of the suggestions. "Throw them out of the commonwealth." I reiterate the view I have expressed before that there is no merit in such action. Such a course may have some superficial attractions but what of its objections? It would respond to natural feelings of distaste for racial policy; it may commend itself for its purgatory effect. What would it solve? Would it bring relief to the 10 million blacks in that country? Would it bring relief to the many whites who do not share the view on discrimination? You are going to throw the 10 million blacks out. The whites who do not hold the same views as the government of the day you are going to throw out into outer darkness. That is what some say.
There is no machinery provided in the commonwealth to do so, as there are no qualifications as to beliefs required for membership in the commonwealth. One of the greatest hopes I have for an ultimate settlement is that South Africa has not withdrawn itself from the commonwealth and the fact that it will be represented in London at the prime ministers' conference assures that the channels of informal communication have not been closed.
Mr. Phillips of the Toronto Star was interviewed by a well-known former member of the press gallery, who tried to get him to say that we should throw South Africa out of the commonwealth. What was his answer? He was asked this question:
Do you think it would be ... do good or harm to most people if we somehow kicked South Africa out of the commonwealth now?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I wouldn't like to see South Africa kicked out of the commonwealth. I've met South Africans who are the same type of people as Canadians and even when I was in jail I talked to a ... I was in prison with a young doctor and I said "Why don't you come to Canada: your career is being blighted here"-and he said "No, my job is to stay in South Africa-I'm very proud of my country and I want to see it have a better future than it's getting."
Phillips spoke with the experience that comes from one who knows. He went on to repeat that.
Then they say "Boycott South Africa." That sounds like something that is attractive to some people. Who would suffer? How many of those who hold that view have any realization of who would suffer? In 1959 Canada's exports to South Africa totalled $51,377,332 while imports from South Africa amounted to $6,631,000. They bought from us eight times what we bought from them. Who would suffer? Members of the C.C.F. party, as reported in the press, talk about kicking a country out of the commonwealth, but I point out that we sold to South Africa $15,642,000 of wheat. South Africa is our fourth largest
3340	HOUSE OF
Apartheid Policy in Commonwealth customer for wheat. Let nobody say that I believe that the cause of freedom should be weighed in the scales of monetary considerations, but I simply ask the question: Who would suffer by the boycott? There are other countries in the commonwealth with quite the reverse situation, whose trade picture is quite different and where the balance of trade is in favour of South Africa.
The next suggestion is that we should make a formal protest. I have already answered that by reference to the attitude taken by the other governments of the commonwealth. So far as our commonwealth governments are concerned, let us exercise an influence of moderation, let us be served by steadiness and restraint, and remember always that this problem did not begin in 1960 but has existed since 1948.
We continue to believe that the clarity and the certainty of the words that we direct to the representatives of that country, coupled with the situation that has arisen as a result of which Mr. Hammarskjold, the Secretary General of the United Nations, will meet with the representative of the prime minister of South Africa at the conference in London and will later go to South Africa, hold the hope that at least there is a realization that something will have to be achieved.
I turn now to the delicate question of how this problem might be dealt with at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference. The house will appreciate that it is impossible to know in what way the matter might arise. I believe it will come about informally, and in informal discussion it is possible to convey the views shown to be in the hearts and souls of hon. members of this house today and of Canadians generally. There is one advantage when you express your views in that way. You do not mobilize the stubbornness which is inherent in all of us. How many of us have reacted to criticism in quite the opposite way to that which the criticism was intented to evoke?
The further question arises whether there should be some corporate expression of condemnation or disapproval. I do not believe that. I think in general that meeting together we shall bring about some realization that within the commonwealth as it expands there will come a day, which cannot be too far removed, when discrimination will not be accepted but rather that there will be a common brotherhood, each country with its own form of government, an anachronism without organization, a family group without treaty or pact and without anything to bind us together which works, as the Leader of the Opposition said; a commonwealth drawing its strength not from sameness but from


diversity, providing the soil and climate in which its individual members can achieve and consolidate self-sustaining growth and the atmosphere in which they can develop talents and capabilities of their own choosing. That is my idea of the commonwealth. It is not something that denies criticism among its members, but that does not mean that it permits of action being taken to exile those of its members with whom the others do not agree. That is not the spirit of the commonwealth.
My time is up and I will conclude if I may have one minute. No problem has caused me more concern. Someone has said that I am torn between what I think is right and, on the other hand, what I think would be appropriate. It is nothing of the kind. I have a horror of discrimination against the individual but that does not mean that I believe in bringing about change by denunciation. That has been tried before. Someone has said that responsibility is rarely easy and for those who are really responsible it is all the more difficult. That has been the situation and I have tried to give leadership to the Canadian people who believe in the commonwealth. There has been no condonation of wrongdoing. I could do the popular thing. I could denounce. I could follow the course of least resistance but denunciation of what I hate would not achieve what we desire should be achieved, the ending of a policy that cannot succeed. Mr. Macmillan spoke of the winds of change. I think of them as hurricanes as men are driven to new heights in their desire for equality and an opportunity for the better things of life. Today in what has been said in the house there has been a freedom from the outcry of political considerations. The debate, which began with leadership, has continued so throughout. For me the debate has been worth while.
